```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(fairy)
# In this vignette all volumes are computed exactly (convex hull), so that the printed
# numbers are deterministic. The package default is a volesti estimate (see ?fairy_volume).
for (f in c("fairy_volume", "fairy_max_bf", "fairy_info", "fairy_compare", "fairy_parsimony", "fairy")) {
  g <- get(f); formals(g)$method <- "exact"; assign(f, g)
}
options(width = 90)
```

**fairy** turns verbal hypotheses about proportions into order-constrained models and answers the
questions the paper "Wait, what are you saying, exactly?" asks of them: What exactly does the
hypothesis say (constraints)? Which extreme cases does it allow? How parsimonious is it? How does it
relate to other models? This page introduces the idea and lists every function. The vignette
`vignette("paper-examples")` then reproduces the paper's examples.

# The idea

A hypothesis about `n` proportions `p1, ..., pn` is a set of linear (in)equalities. Together they
describe a convex polytope inside the unit cube `[0, 1]^n`. The package describes that polytope in two
equivalent ways:

* the **H-representation**: the shortest list of constraints (equalities and facet-defining inequalities);
* the **V-representation**: the extreme cases (vertices) of the model.

Its **volume** is the share of all conceivable proportions the model allows (the smaller, the more restrictive and more precise the model); its inverse is the
largest Bayes factor the model can reach against the unconstrained model.

# Writing a model

A model is one character string. Constraints are separated by `;`.

| Write | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `p1 > p2` | `p1` at least `p2` (`>=` and the unicode symbol mean the same: models are closed sets) |
| `p1 > p2 > p3` | chain: `p1 > p2` and `p2 > p3` |
| `p1 = p2` | equality (the model then has volume zero) |
| `p1 > .3; p1 < .7` | bounds |
| `{p1, p2} > {p3, p4}` | every `p` on the left above every `p` on the right |
| `(p1 + p2)/2 > p3` | averages and other linear expressions |

`approx_tol = 0.05` (in `fairy_h()`) turns every equality into "within 0.05".

# Constraints and extreme cases

```{r hv}
h <- fairy_h("p1 > p2 > p3", n_p = 3)     # H-representation (rcdd format)
fairy_constraints(h)                       # the same, as readable text
fairy_vertices(h)                          # extreme cases, numbers
fairy_words(h, labels = c("A", "B", "C"))  # extreme cases in words: "all" / "none"
```

## How to read the H- and V-description

Both describe the same set of allowed probability combinations (a polytope), from two sides:

* **H-description (constraints).** Each row is one constraint, and the model is the set of all combinations that satisfy
  *all* rows at once. `p2 <= p1` says that `p2` is at most `p1`; a row of type `equality` fixes a relation exactly. Constraints
  that are redundant are left out; the bounds 0 <= p <= 1 appear only where they restrict the model (e.g. `p1 <= 1`).
* **V-description (extreme cases).** Each row is a vertex: an allowed combination that cannot be written as a mixture of
  two other allowed combinations. Every allowed combination is a weighted mixture of the rows.

`fairy_h_table()` and `fairy_v_table()` put them into tables, and `fairy_table_write()` turns a table into Markdown, LaTeX or CSV:

```{r tables}
fairy_h_table(h)
fairy_h_table(h, style = "paper")    # the form of the paper's Figure 2: - p1 + p2 <= 0
fairy_h_table(h, style = "matrix")   # a1*p1 + ... + an*pn <= b, one row per constraint
fairy_v_table(h)
fairy_table_write(fairy_v_table(h, words = TRUE))
```

`fairy_v(h)` returns the vertices in rcdd's own format. `fairy_dim()` gives the dimension of the model.
Models with an equality have a dimension below `n` and volume zero:

```{r dim}
c(fairy_dim("p1 > p2 > p3"), fairy_dim("p1 = p2; p2 > p3"))
```

# Starting from a model you already have

You never need to recompute a model. Every function accepts a model string, an H-representation from
`fairy_h()`, **or** a V-representation (the vertices): pass `h` or `v` straight to `fairy_volume()`,
`fairy_max_bf()`, `fairy_info()`, `fairy_nested()`, `fairy_compare()`, `fairy_replicate()` and so on.

```{r reuse}
v <- fairy_v(h)                  # V-representation in rcdd format
fairy_max_bf(v)                  # the same as fairy_max_bf(h)
```

If you only have your own table of vertices (one row per extreme case, probabilities as numbers or exact
fractions such as `"1/3"`), `fairy_from_vertices()` turns it into the H-representation:

```{r from-vertices}
corners <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 0), c(1, 1))      # a triangle
h_tri <- fairy_from_vertices(corners)
fairy_constraints(h_tri)
fairy_volume(h_tri)$volume
```

# Parsimony

```{r parsimony}
fairy_volume("p1 > p2 > p3")$volume          # 1/6
fairy_max_bf("p1 > p2 > p3")                 # 6
fairy_info("p1 > p2 > p3")                   # dimension, vertices, constraints, volume, max. BF in one row
```

Outside this vignette, `fairy_volume()` by default estimates the volume with the volesti package and its own default settings; any non-default volesti option can be passed via `...` (e.g. `settings = list(error = 0.01)`). `method = "exact"` (convex hull of the vertices) and `method = "mc"` (Monte Carlo) are available on request. `fairy_parsimony()` is the older name of the same computation.

## The same as in the app: exact first, estimate after a time limit

The **Shiny app** calculates the exact volume first (it is a number such as 1/6, not an estimate) and uses an algorithm only for the models that
have no exact volume or whose exact volume takes more than five minutes. In the package this is `method = "auto"`:

```{r auto}
v <- fairy::fairy_volume("p1 > p2 > p3", n_p = 3, method = "auto", time_limit = 300)   # the original function (this vignette fixes the default of fairy_volume() to "exact")
v$volume                                     # 1/6, exact
v$method                                     # "exact": it finished within the time limit
```

When the exact calculation takes longer than `time_limit` seconds (it runs in a separate R process that is stopped, which needs the package
callr), `method = "auto"` returns the volesti estimate, and `$method` says so (`"volesti (the exact volume took too long)"`). Nothing else
switches the method on its own: the default stays `"volesti"`, because the exact volume can take very long in high dimensions
(up to about 10 dimensions it is usually quick, with 12 and more it can take minutes or longer).

# Several models at once

`fairy()` computes constraints, extreme cases, volume and maximal Bayes factor for a named set of models:

```{r fairy}
fairy(c(H1 = "p1 > p2 > p3", H2 = "p1 > p2; p3 > p4"), n_p = 4)
```

# Overlap, nesting, mixtures, comparison

```{r combine}
a <- "p1 > p2 > p3"; b <- "p1 > p2"
fairy_nested(a, b, n_p = 3)                  # is a nested in b?  TRUE
ab <- fairy_intersect(a, b, n_p = 3)         # constraints of both hold
mx <- fairy_mixture("p1 > .8; p2 < .2", "p1 < .2; p2 > .8", n_p = 2)   # convex hull of two models
fairy_constraints(mx)
fairy_compare(list(A = a, B = b, C = "p3 > p1"), n_p = 3)        # volumes, overlaps, nesting, max. BF
```

`fairy_compare()` returns the table layout of the paper: volumes on the diagonal, overlap volumes above it,
below it "subset" / "superset" (printed as the set symbols) or the dimension of the overlap, and the largest
Bayes factors in the last row.

## Which extreme cases do models share?

`fairy_compare_vertices()` lists, for every extreme case of every model, in which other models it is also an extreme case, and which
ones only this model has (the Compare buttons of the app):

```{r vertices}
r <- fairy_compare_vertices(list(A = a, B = b, C = "p3 > p1"), n_p = 3)
r                                            # per model: vertices, shared, unique
head(r$vertices, 4)                          # per vertex: the models that share it
```

An intersection or a mixture is compared like in the app: ordinary models only with each other, and a model named in `derived` with all
ordinary models except, for a mixture, its own components (its extreme cases are theirs by construction; name them in `components`).

# Replication across labs

```{r replicate}
h2 <- fairy_h("p1 > p2", n_p = 2)
fairy_info(fairy_replicate(h2, r = 3, type = "joint"))
```

`type = "identical"` forces all labs to have the same probabilities, `"joint"` lets each lab satisfy the
model independently, `"substitutable"` requires every constraint to hold whichever lab's probability is plugged in for each
term.

# Unpacking across items

`fairy_replicate()` repeats the whole model the same way for every lab. `fairy_unpack()` is the general form: probabilities can have
different numbers of items, can share an item list, and each list says in its own way how the theory holds across its items
(`"joint"` item by item, `"substitutable"` for every combination, `"identical"` for a shared value, within a tolerance `eps`, or
`"average"` for the average over the items).

```{r unpack}
# p1 and p2 share a list of 2 items, p3 has its own list of 3 items
h3 <- fairy_unpack("p3 > p1 + p2", items = c(2, 2, 3), lists = c("A", "A", "B"),
                   type = c(A = "substitutable", B = "average"), n_p = 3)
colnames(h3)[-(1:2)]
```

Unpacked models with the same number of items for every probability live in the same space, also when the items are grouped
differently, and can be combined. `fairy_intersect()`, `fairy_mixture()`, `fairy_nested()` and `fairy_compare()` match their
columns by name. The package only checks that the numbers of items fit; that item *k* of one probability means the same thing as
item *k* of another is up to you.

```{r unpack-combine}
m <- fairy_h("p1 > p2; p2 > p3", n_p = 3)
avg  <- fairy_unpack(m, items = 2, type = "average")
subs <- fairy_unpack(m, items = 2, lists = c("A", "B", "C"), type = "substitutable")
fairy_nested(subs, avg)                # every combination of items implies the average
fairy_info(fairy_intersect(avg, subs), volume = FALSE)
```

# Export

`fairy_write_qtest()` and `fairy_write_multinomineq()` write the models as input files for QTEST and for the R package
multinomineq (one `.tar` archive with one file per model). The files are the same as the downloads of the app.

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
mods <- c(H1 = "p1 > p2 > p3", H2 = "p1 > p2; p2 = p3")
fairy_write_qtest(mods, n_p = 3, file = "qtest.tar")
fairy_write_multinomineq(mods, n_p = 3, file = "multinomineq.tar")
```

* **Order of the probabilities:** `order = list(H1 = c(3, 1, 2))` makes the third probability the first column of the files of `H1`
  (QTEST and multinomineq may expect another order than you wrote the model in). Models that are not listed keep their own order.
* **Equalities:** an equality between two probabilities (`p2 = p3`) is merged into one column for multinomineq and listed in
  `map_<model>.csv` (the `map` argument of multinomineq); QTEST cannot express equalities, so the file lists them in an extra block with a
  note. Any other equality gives volume zero.
* **Numbers:** constants stay exact fractions (`1/3`, `0.0001`) up to the files; nothing goes through a floating-point step.

## Analysing data with multinomineq

The multinomineq archive also contains your data, the settings of the analysis and a script, `analysis_multinomineq.R`, that analyses
every model in its folder and writes `results.csv` (Bayes factors against the unconstrained model and against the model's complement),
`posterior.csv` (estimates of the probabilities) and `results.html` (the main results as a web page):

```{r analysis, eval = FALSE}
dat <- data.frame(probability = c("p1", "p2", "p3"), n = c(30, 30, 45), frequency = c(21, 12, 9))
fairy_write_multinomineq(mods, n_p = 3, file = "multinomineq.tar", data = dat,
                         settings = list(posterior_samples = 5000, bf_samples = 10000,
                                         burnin_post = 10, burnin_bf = 5, prior = c(1, 1), seed = 1234))
```

`data` has one row per probability (`n` observations, `frequency` how often the outcome was observed); the numbers belong to the
probability's name, so they stay with it when `order` changes. A list named by model gives that model its own file
(`data_model_<name>.csv`, for unpacked models whose probabilities mean something of their own); without `data` the archive contains example
numbers that you replace. `fairy_multinomineq_script()` returns the text of the script alone.

To run the analysis directly from R (needs the packages multinomineq and coda), use `fairy_analyze_multinomineq()`:

```{r run, eval = FALSE}
res <- fairy_analyze_multinomineq(mods, n_p = 3, data = dat, settings = list(seed = 1))
res$results      # Bayes factors
res$posterior    # estimates of the probabilities
res$report       # path of results.html
```

The Bayes factors depend on the prior (`prior = c(1, 1)` is the uniform prior on every probability), and the estimates have a Monte Carlo
error: for the final numbers use more samples (`bf_samples`) and report the seed.

# All functions

| Function | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| `fairy()` | constraints, extreme cases, volume and max. Bayes factor for one or several models |
| `fairy_h()` | non-redundant H-representation of a model string |
| `fairy_v()` | V-representation in rcdd format |
| `fairy_from_vertices()` | H-representation from a table of vertices (V to H) |
| `fairy_constraints()` | H-representation as readable text lines |
| `fairy_vertices()` | extreme cases as a numeric matrix |
| `fairy_words()` | extreme cases in words ("all" / "none" / fractions) |
| `fairy_h_table()`, `fairy_v_table()` | H- and V-description as tables (`fairy_table_write()`: Markdown, LaTeX, CSV) |
| `fairy_dim()` | dimension of a model |
| `fairy_volume()` | parsimony: volume in the unit cube (exact, volesti, Monte Carlo, or `"auto"`: exact first as in the app) |
| `fairy_max_bf()` | largest possible Bayes factor against the unconstrained model (1 / volume) |
| `fairy_info()` | dimension, vertices, constraints, volume, max. Bayes factor in one row |
| `fairy_parsimony()` | older interface to the volume |
| `fairy_intersect()` | intersection of models |
| `fairy_mixture()` | mixture model (convex hull of the components) |
| `fairy_nested()` | is one model nested in another? |
| `fairy_compare()` | comparison table of a set of models (Table 3 of the paper) |
| `fairy_replicate()` | replication across labs: identical, joint, substitutable |
| `fairy_unpack()` | unpacking across items: lists, joint / substitutable / identical (with tolerance) / average |
| `fairy_compare_vertices()` | which extreme cases do models share, which are unique to a model |
| `fairy_write_qtest()` | write input files for QTEST |
| `fairy_write_multinomineq()` | write input files for multinomineq: models, data, settings and the analysis script |
| `fairy_multinomineq_script()` | text of the analysis script of the multinomineq archive |
| `fairy_analyze_multinomineq()` | run the multinomineq analysis from R: Bayes factors and posterior estimates |

Help for any function: `?fairy_volume`; all of them: `help(package = "fairy")`.
